tagline: Water-powered mills and brick housing trace the making of Manchester
intro: The Amoskeag Millyard Scenic and Cultural Byway runs through Manchester, New Hampshire; FHWA lists it as one mile long and emphasizes the city’s cultural and historic attractions. Scenic America’s 2023 New Hampshire inventory includes it among the state scenic byways. Elm Street follows a ridge parallel to the mills below.

In 1807, Samuel Blodgett completed a canal and locks that let boats bypass Amoskeag Falls. The manufacturing company later bought east-bank land for mills, canals and a town. Its bankruptcy came in 1935; renovated mills now hold offices, restaurants, college branches and a museum.

At the northern end of the mill district, District D places worker rowhouses below an overseer’s house. District C lies between Hollis and Bridge streets. The Millyard Museum occupies Mill No. 3 at 200 Bedford Street.

moments.title: District D
moments.text: At District D, the slope helped organize company housing: workers lived nearest the mills, overseers farther uphill, and the agent at the top. Built in 1864, the brick worker rowhouses have mansard roofs and stepped units that accommodate the terrain. The agent’s house is gone; a twentieth-century warehouse now separates the overseer’s building from the worker tenements.

moments.title: District C
moments.text: Brick rowhouses in District C stand east of the former mills and west of Elm Street. Their entrances pair beneath Stick style hoods, and dormers interrupt the hip roofs. The company’s last housing group was built here in 1916 for overseers. The buildings became condominiums in the 1970s.

moments.title: Mill No. 3
moments.text: Manchester Historic Association tells the city’s history inside Mill No. 3, home of the Millyard Museum. The factory complex depended on power from Amoskeag Falls on the Merrimack River. After the company went bankrupt in 1935, the mill site went through abandonment, demolition and redevelopment.
